title: Four summaries
hook: the world is swept away, has no protector, owns nothing, is a slave to craving

segments.voice: Yesterday: Raṭṭhapāla's fast, and the only son who came home as he promised and kindly said no to the gold. Your line: he stood by it.

Same sutta, second half. Raṭṭhapāla has left his family's house and is sitting under a tree in the king's park. King Koravya comes out for a stroll, recognizes him, and sits down with real curiosity. People go forth, the king says, for four reasons: they're old, or sick, or they've lost their money, or they've lost their family. You're young. You're healthy. Your family is rich and alive. So why? It's a fair question, the kind a friend asks over coffee when you've quit a good job.
screen: `UNDER A TREE IN THE KING'S PARK.` → `OLD, SICK, BROKE, OR BEREAVED?` → `NONE OF THEM. SO WHY?`

segments.voice: Raṭṭhapāla answers with four short sayings he heard from the Buddha, which he calls summaries of the teaching. One: the world is swept away; it does not last. Two: the world has no shelter, no one in charge to protect it. Three: the world owns nothing; you have to leave everything and go on. Four: the world is never full, never satisfied, a slave to craving. Then he asks the king four questions, one for each. At twenty-five, how were you at riding, at archery, with a sword? Strong, says the king; sometimes I thought I had no equal. And now? Now I'm eighty. Sometimes I mean to step one way and my foot goes another. That's the first: swept away. Do you have an illness? Wind trouble, says the king. When it comes, can your ministers and relatives take some of the pain for you? No. I have to feel it all alone. Second: no shelter. These treasures, will you take them with you? No. Third: you own nothing. And last: if a trusted man came from the east and said there's a rich country there you could conquer, would you? Yes. And beyond the ocean? Yes, that too. Fourth: never full. Raṭṭhapāla doesn't preach at the king. He lets the king's own life answer. The four summaries aren't meant to make the world look grim. In this sutta they're the reason a young man with everything chose a simpler life, and they're true of kings too.
screen: `SWEPT AWAY: AT TWENTY-FIVE, AND AT EIGHTY.` · `NO SHELTER: NOBODY FEELS YOUR PAIN.` · `OWNS NOTHING: YOU LEAVE IT ALL.` · `NEVER FULL: AND BEYOND THE OCEAN?` · then, large: `THE WORLD IS SWEPT AWAY.`

segments.voice: Choose one of the four, swept away, no shelter, owns nothing, or never full, and let it touch something real: how your body has changed in ten years, a pain only you could feel, a thing you'll leave behind, a want that keeps moving. Don't push for a feeling. Let the summary be true for a few breaths, and notice what softens.
Four summaries. The world is swept away, has no shelter, owns nothing, and is never full. Raṭṭhapāla's answer to a king who asked why he left.
Your line: the world is swept away. Strong at twenty-five, unsteady at eighty, even for a king. Day four hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners reflect regularly on impermanence and the limits of possessions, and teachers use Raṭṭhapāla's four summaries as a short framework for that reflection.

original.note: Pali: 'the world is swept away; it does not last.' the first of the four summaries.

trapdoor: what you thought: the world is swept away sounds like a disaster.
what it means: nothing in life stands still: strength, health, possessions and wants all move.
what a scholar hears: MN 82's four dhammuddesas, 'summaries of the teaching', are each illustrated by a question to King Koravya and closed with Raṭṭhapāla's verses.
recall: the thus-gone one, a title for the Buddha

chat.says: Why would a young, healthy, rich person leave it all for a monk's life?
options: His four reasons: the world is swept away, unsheltered, owns nothing, and is never full.
Only because something went wrong: age, sickness, debt or losing family.
Raṭṭhapāla said he left because his parents refused him their gold.
chat.meaning: In MN 82 Raṭṭhapāla gives King Koravya four summaries of the teaching, and lets the king's own life show each one.

Raṭṭhapāla.meaning: an only son who went forth as a monk

Koravya.meaning: the king who asked Raṭṭhapāla why he went forth

go forth.meaning: to leave home for the life of a monk or nun
